item.title: Where’s the Guernica of the Ukraine war?
item.description:
In the aftermath of Putin’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine up to a million of Russia’s brightest and best fled into exile. Among them were a significant proportion of the country’s leading theatre and film directors, writers and artists. Surely such a cataclysm as Russia’s descent into madness and fascism would generate an epochal and tragic artistic response from these thousands of talented exiles?
Alas, anyone looking for a contemporary equivalent of Picasso’s ‘Guernica’, Koestler’s Darkness at Noon or Costa-Gavras’s Z will not find it among the work of today’s Russian émigrés.

item.title: Britain should be ashamed of its sham universities
item.description:
Nestled in an industrial estate just outside Coventry, Arden University might well be Britain’s most inconspicuous educational establishment. But if you consider a university to be a business (and Arden clearly does), it is arguably the best performing in the country. The figures are striking: Arden was given the permanent power to award degrees in 2021 and over the past decade has expanded its headcount from 2,000 students to just over 32,000. In other words, once a minnow, it now has more students than either Oxford or Cambridge.
That’s not all. Unlike almost every other university in the country, Arden is a private, for-profit institution. Last year, it made a post-tax profit of over £64.

item.title: From Brussels with love: they’ve been expecting you, Mr Burnham
item.description:
The day after Vote Leave’s victory in the 2016 EU referendum, the campaign director Dominic Cummings turned to a colleague and said: ‘It’s great. We’ve taken back control. The only thing that worries me is who we’re handing control back to.’ This week, that colleague reflected on the ‘prescience’ of these words.
Polls show voters do not believe Brexit was handled well over the past decade – something which Andy Burnham has used to justify thrusting Brexit back onto the political battleground. ‘For me it’s déjà-vu on steroids,’ says Nigel Farage who, like a lot of Brexit-eers this week, seems torn between outrage and excitement at the need to get back in the arena and fight. ‘Burnham has decided to poison the well of British politics.’

item.description: In the Aeneid, after the purported departure of the Greeks, the Trojans find two things left behind: a great wooden horse and a Greek soldier named Sinon. Sinon is brought before King Priam of Troy. He tells an emotive story about being persecuted at the hands of his enemies while imploring the Trojans to accept the wooden horse into the city, promising that it is a gift from Minerva. Priam is so moved by Sinon’s story that he tells him: ‘Whoever you are, forget the Greeks lost to you, you’ll be one of us.’ That night, now unchained and trusted to walk the city, Sinon opens the wooden horse and out comes a group of hardened soldiers, who set about burning and razing his supposed sanctuary.

item.title: The prison early release scheme is already a disaster
item.description:
Four days after he was released from HMP Wandsworth, Michael Bogle was back inside. The 38-year-old had served 11 of 32 weeks in prison for stealing before he was freed last month via the government’s early release scheme. He strolled out of jail, told reporters he would ‘hopefully not’ shoplift again, then stole from a Sainsbury’s a few hours later.
The early release scheme was meant to increase prison capacity. But it isn’t working. Since it began two years ago, 80,000 people have been freed, yet there are just 1,000 extra prison spaces. Last week, the Ministry of Justice revealed that more offenders were recalled to jail in the first half of this year (25,531) than were let out (25,255).
